elements.id-string-3: Cancer development is associated with aberrant DNA methylation, including increased stochastic variability.
elements.id-string-4: Statistical tests for discovering cancer methylation biomarkers have focused on changes in mean methylation.
elements.id-string-5: To improve the power of  detection, we propose to incorporate increased variability in testing for cancer differential methylation by two joint constrained tests: one for differential mean and increased variance, the other for increased mean and increased variance.
elements.id-string-6: To improve small sample properties, likelihood ratio statistics are developed, accounting for the variability in estimating the sample medians in the Levene test.
elements.id-string-7: Efficient algorithms were developed and  implemented in \texttt{DMVC} function of {\bf R} package \texttt{DMtest}.
elements.id-string-8: The proposed joint constrained tests were compared to standard tests and partial area under the curve (pAUC) for the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) in simulated datasets under diverse models.
elements.id-string-9: Application to the high-throughput methylome data in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) shows substantially increased yield of candidate CpG markers.
elements.id-string-10: \keywords{Cancer biomarker discovery; CpG methylation; Constrained hypothesis; Differential variance; Joint test; Levene test}
elements.id-string-12: Cancer development is associated with profound modifications in the epigenome, a multi-layer regulatory infrastructure for gene expression and cellular lineage \citep{Esteller2007,Esteller2008,Baylin2011,Shen2013a}.
elements.id-string-13: The most studied cancer epigenetic alteration to date is the 5-cytosine methylation at CpG dinucleotides.
elements.id-string-14: Occurring early in carcinogenesis and biochemically more stable than RNA transcripts, aberrant DNA methylation has become an important molecular target for developing cancer early detection marker \citep{Laird2003,Issa2008}.
elements.id-string-15: High-throughput assays such as the Illumina Infinium HumanMethylation450, EPIC BeadChips and whole genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) enable interrogation of cancer methylome for CpG biomarker candidates \citep{Hao2017}.
elements.id-string-16: The current statistical engine for detecting cancer aberrant methylation entails testing equal means between cancer and normal samples for a single CpG site (differentially methylated CpG, {\bf DMC}) or a region with multiple adjacent CpGs (differentially methylated region, {\bf DMR}), as implemented in popular software such as \texttt{Minfi} \citep{Aryee2014} and \texttt{ChAMP} \citep{Morris2014}.
elements.id-string-17: The high dimensionality of genome-wide CpGs ($>$500,000) and typically small sample size for biomarker discovery studies limit the statistical power to identify novel markers.
elements.id-string-19: Differential cancer methylation is also evident by increased stochastic variability.
elements.id-string-20: This has been observed across cancers \citep{Hansen2011,Phipson2014}, which may reflect adaptation to local tumor environments in the carcinogenesis process.
elements.id-string-21: Testing for equal variances in sample groups has been studied in the statistical literature for decades \citep{Brown1974}.
elements.id-string-22: Levene test achieves a balance between sensitivity and robustness to outliers, therefore has been used for detecting differentially variable CpG ({\bf DVC}) \citep{Phipson2014}.
elements.id-string-23: Figure \ref{volcano_plot_six_cancers}  shows the volcano plots for testing differential variability in six major cancers available in TCGA using Levene test: namely prostate cancer (PCa),  colorectal cancer (CRC), lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD),  breast cancer (BRCA), and liver hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
elements.id-string-24: A striking observation is that nearly all DVCs show increased variability in cancer samples ($>$99\% in BRCA, CRC, HCC, LUSC and LUAD, $>$95\% in PCa), confirming that cancer DVC is ubiquitously hypervariable.

elements.id-string-27: In this work, we develop joint tests that combine differential means and increased variances in CpG methylation data, aiming to improve the power of detecting cancer biomarker candidates.
elements.id-string-28: Specifically gearing to the ubiquitously increased variability in cancer DNA methylation, we develop two constrained hypothesis tests: a test for {\bf differential} mean and {\bf increased} variance, and another test for {\bf increased} mean and {\bf increased} variance.
elements.id-string-29: We used the estimating equation theory and likelihood ratio tests for constrained hypothesis to construct test statistics.
elements.id-string-30: We found that the variability in estimating the medians in Levene test needs to be accounted for in test statistics, in order to achieve better control of the type I error rate for high dimensional p-values.
elements.id-string-31: Computationally efficient algorithms for these tests were developed in the \texttt{DMVC} function of {\bf R} package \texttt{DMtest}, which is capable of scanning 500,000 CpGs for biomarker leads in a few minutes.
elements.id-string-32: Another goal of this work is to compare the proposed constrained joint tests to the partial area under the curve (pAUC) measure for receiver operating characteristics curve (ROC), that is commonly used in the biomarker literature for selecting cancer gene expression markers \citep{Pepe2003}.
elements.id-string-33: In a similar one-sided fashion, pAUC evaluates the discriminative performance between cancers and controls in the high specificity area of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.
elements.id-string-34: In simulated datasets, we compare error control and power performance of pAUC, the standard t-test, Levene test, and the proposed constrained tests in diverse models.
elements.id-string-35: The utility of the proposed constrained tests for biomarker discovery will be investigated by TCGA methylome data.

elements.id-string-168: To evaluate the power of the proposed constrained method in a single hypothesis test, four scenarios were generated with 50 cases and 50 controls, each with some distributional differences between cancer samples and control samples.
elements.id-string-169: We included pAUC in this power comparison despite its problem in high-dimensional testing, because the p-value cut-off 0.05 for pAUC still yields a valid type I error rate.
elements.id-string-170: Methylation M values were generated by a Gaussian distribution or a mixture of Gaussian distributions.
elements.id-string-171: A parameter $\tau \in$ [0,0.7] was used to control the magnitude of the differences:  the first scenario is all cancer samples having both mean and variance increase, specifically $\mathcal{N}(\tau,1+\tau)$ vs $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ ; the second scenario is all cancer samples having increased variance but no difference in mean, specifically $\mathcal{N}(0,1+\tau)$ vs $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$; the third scenario is all cancer samples having mean increase but no difference in variance , specifically $\mathcal{N}(\tau,1)$ vs $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$; the fourth scenario is 25\% cancer samples with increasing mean and variance, specifically a mixture of 75\% $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and 25\%  $\mathcal{N}(3\tau,1+3\tau)$.
elements.id-string-172: Figure \ref{power_plot_simulations} shows the power to reject the null hypothesis (no differential methylation in mean nor variance) in 2,000 simulated datasets for the proposed constrained joint tests and the benchmark methods.
elements.id-string-173: In all scenarios the joint constrained test for $H_{1c}$ (increased mean and increased variance) delivered consistently the highest power, owing to its flexibility in detecting diverse signals (as compared to t-test or Levine test) and its focus on one-sided alternative hypotheses (as compared to the 2-df test).
elements.id-string-174: More restriction in the alternative parameter space increases the power, as seen from the comparison of the constrained tests for H$_{1b}$ and H$_{1c}$.
elements.id-string-175: The test for pAUC(0.2) performs competitively in the first scenario where there is both mean and variance increase, and in the fourth scenario where there is a subgroup with increased mean and variance.
elements.id-string-176: However when there is only increased mean or only increased variance, pAUC is clearly inferior to the proposed constrained test.

elements.id-string-179: Methylome data by the Infinium Methylation 450K assay for 2781 fresh-frozen tumor tissue samples were obtained from TCGA for 6 major cancers, namely prostate cancer (PCa),  colorectal cancer (CRC), lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD),  breast cancer (BRCA), and liver hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and 308 matched adjacent normal samples.
elements.id-string-180: The sample sizes for each cancer and its matched normal samples are shown in Table \ref{all_DMresults}.
elements.id-string-181: Differential variability was first examined, comparing the six major cancers to their corresponding normal tissue samples.
elements.id-string-182: Low variability CpG sites, defined to be those with standard deviation of beta values $<$0.05 in the combined cancer and matched normal samples, were considered to be noninformative and filtered out before analyses.
elements.id-string-183: A regression based approach is undertaken to assess homogeneity of variances of methylation M values between cancer and normal samples, essentially the classical Levene test for differential variability \citep{Brown1974,Phipson2014} and adjusting for age (and gender when applicable).
elements.id-string-184: Figure \ref{volcano_plot_six_cancers} shows the volcano plots for genome-wide DVC test results in the six cancers, where the x axis is the difference of standard deviation of methylation beta values.
elements.id-string-185: At the family-wise error rate (FWER) 0.05, there are 21220 (PCa), 54734 (CRC), 76455 (LUSC), 31817 (LUAD), 120073 (BRCA), and 132797 (HCC) significant DVCs for the six cancers respectively.
elements.id-string-186: Nearly all DVCs show increased variability in cancer samples ($>$99\% in BRCA, CRC, HCC, LUSC and LUAD, $>$95\% in PCa).
elements.id-string-187: Compared to the number of significant DMCs (Table \ref{all_DMresults}), liver cancer has more DVCs and breast cancer has a similar number of DVCs (Table \ref{all_DMresults}), probably because of several distinctive subtypes in these two cancers.

elements.id-string-190: A large portion of significant DVCs were not detected as significant DMCs, varying from  25\% to 53\% across 6 cancers (Table \ref{all_DMresults}), which suggests that testing for DVCs can increase the chance of detecting cancer aberrant methylation beyond DMCs.
elements.id-string-191: Figure \ref{four_examples} shows four examples of significant DVCs with low methylation in normal samples, but not detected as significant DMCs.
elements.id-string-192: In all CpG examples, violin plots for beta values and the density plots for M values show that there is a hypermethylated subgroup separating from the rest of samples that have similar methylation as the normal samples.
elements.id-string-193: These CpGs indexing heterogenous cancer subgroups may be better detected by testing for differential variability, since the p-values for testing DVCs are typically much smaller than the p-values for DMC.
elements.id-string-194: Interestingly, every one of these CpGs can discriminate cancer samples from normal samples with AUC$>$0.7, achieving a sensitivity $>$0.4 at nearly 100\% specificity.
elements.id-string-195: These DVCs have potential to delineate the heterogeneity in cancer methylome, and to be candidate cancer early detection markers when combined in a multi-marker panel.

elements.id-string-197: We used the two constrained joint tests for differential mean and increased variable (hypervariable) as expressed in H$_{1b}$ and H$_{1c}$ for the six TCGA cancer-normal comparisons.
elements.id-string-198: For testing H$_{1b}$, a substantial higher amount of CpGs show FWER $<$0.05 than the numbers for DMC, e.g., nearly three times as much as DMCs for LUAD, 50\% more for LUSC.
elements.id-string-199: In biomarker discovery studies, the interest is often more on the CpGs that are not methylated in normal samples (mean beta $<$0.1) to protect specificity, but hypermethylated in cancer samples.
elements.id-string-200: Across 6 comparisons, the constrained joint test for  H$_{1c}$ identified substantially more significant hypermethylated CpGs than the standard DMC test, generally 20-40\% more and as many as 3-fold drastic increase for HCC (Table \ref{all_DMresults}).
elements.id-string-201: This is perhaps not surprising given we observed the widespread increase of variances in cancer CpGs in Figure \ref{volcano_plot_six_cancers}.
elements.id-string-203: Testing for differential methylation between two sample groups has been the analytical workhorse of methylation studies.
elements.id-string-204: The methodological contribution of this work is integrating differences of means and increased variances into joint constrained hypothesis tests, motivated by the observation that DVCs are predominantly hypervariable in all six cancers in TCGA (Figure \ref{volcano_plot_six_cancers}).
elements.id-string-205: This strategy improves the power to identify cancer-specific CpGs in a genome-wide interrogation.
elements.id-string-206: As illustrated by the TCGA data example, exploiting increased variances increases the yield of candidate CpG markers.
elements.id-string-207: When studying DVCs in the six common cancers from TCGA, one of the most interesting observations is that these DVCs often present heterogenous subgroups in cancer patients (Figure \ref{four_examples}), that may not been detected as DMCs with adequate significance due to multiple-testing adjustment.
elements.id-string-208: This reiterates the importance of accounting for cancer heterogeneity and subgroups when studying molecular markers.
elements.id-string-209: Similar objectives have been considered by using pAUC for detecting the presence of cancer subgroup for gene expression \citep{Pepe2003}.
elements.id-string-210: In simulations, we showed that accurate variance estimate of pAUC typically requires a large sample size, that testing pAUC in a high-dimensional setting may have an inflated type I error rate.
elements.id-string-211: In contrast, the proposed joint test with constrained hypothesis has better small-sample behaviors and consistently deliver the best power in diverse simulation scenarios.
elements.id-string-212: Another potential utility of the joint test of differential mean and increased variance for DNA methylation is to use the derived CpGs for clustering analysis to define cancer subtypes.
elements.id-string-213: This objective has been universal for large-scale, genome-wide cancer methylation analyses, e.g. TCGA analyses.
elements.id-string-214: The standard starting point for clustering analysis is to extract the most variable top 5000 CpGs and feed them into a clustering algorithm.
elements.id-string-215: The constrained tests based on the cancer-normal comparison may yield a more informative set of cancer-specific markers, because they may capture the subgroups as we showed in Figure \ref{four_examples}.
